newsitem.title: USA: Native Alaskans fight Exxon Valdez's return.
newsitem.headline: Native Alaskans fight Exxon Valdez's return.

text.p: A group of Native Alaskans filed arguments opposing Exxon Corp' effort to return the Exxon Valdez, which spewed millions of gallons of oil into Alaska' Prince William Sound in 1989, to Alaska waters.
A judge's conference in U.S. District Court here was set for Thursday on Exxon's lawsuit to lift a government ban on the Exxon Valdez's return to Alaska waters.

The Valdez, redubbed the Exxon Mediterranean, has been transporting oil from Egypt to European ports. It spilled some 11 million gallons of oil in the Prince William Sound when it hit a reef, causing an environmental disaster from which the sound has not recovered.

The Oil Pollution Act of 1990, passed in response to the Valdez spill, says tankers that have spilled more than 1 million gallons of oil into a marine environment cannot operate in the Prince William Sound.
Exxon is asking a U.S. District judge to lift that ban, saying it is unconstitutional to bar the Valdez from sailing in Alaska waters.

An Exxon spokesman said the company has been operating the tanker at a loss in foreign waters because it is a Jones Act vessel, which means it was built at a higher cost in a U.S. shipyard and must be manned by higher-paid U.S. crews.
Exxon filed lawsuits in March in Houston seeking to overturn the ban.
Lawyers for the Alaska natives group called Exxon's effort "not only highly offensive, but a direct insult to the Native people."

"Eight years of litigation, a $20 million settlement with the Alaska Natives, and a $5 billion punitive damage verdict against it have done little to change Exxon's view that the Alaska Natives living in the area of Prince William Sound court for nothing," attorneys for the Native Alaskans, Michael Hausfeld and Gary Mason, said in a statment.
